# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

**The search window is too small to rank rules.** It is
`r p6_fn(p6_universe$n_val_races)` races. Cross-half rank correlations within
every family run between
`r p6_fcor(min(p6_guard_summary$spearman))` and
`r p6_fcor(max(p6_guard_summary$spearman))` (@sec-found), and the rule that
won the search on both halves reversed by
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (p6_row(p6_round3_ranks$table, "win", "P4 / field size 11-12")$val_roi - p6_row(p6_round3_ranks$table, "win", "P4 / field size 11-12")$test_roi))`
points out of sample. Nothing in this paper should be read as having
identified a good rule.

**The win market does not transfer from it.** Search-set rank predicts test
rank negatively on all four markets. Round 2's positive place-market
correlation did not replicate here, and the difference between the two rounds
is which seven rules happened to be in the shortlist.

**Several rules were read against one test split with no multiplicity
correction.** Twenty-eight rule-by-market combinations were scored on the same
`r p6_fn(p6_universe$n_test_races)` races in one pass. The intervals reported
are marginal 90% race-level bootstraps and are not adjusted for having looked
twenty-eight times. Whatever tops a test table here is partly noise, and the
two rules that did top them — the market favourite and Owen's rule — were
carried forward unconditionally rather than selected, which is the only
reason their position is worth anything at all.

**Only the betting rule is clean.** The model was not selected on these test
races in any single step, but it was selected with knowledge of them across
five papers: the feature set, the objective, the function class, the encoder
architecture and the rung ladder were each chosen after seeing test results
from the papers before. The test split has been scored once per paper, six
times in total, on the same races. Paper 6 fits nothing and refits nothing,
so its betting rules are genuinely out of sample with respect to this split;
the model underneath them is not, and the fair-book columns in @sec-found
inherit that.

**The going and class sub-families were not really tested.**
`r p6_fn(sum(p6_rc_pruned$n_races[p6_rc_pruned$family == "going" & grepl("<= 4", p6_rc_pruned$label)]))`
of `r p6_fn(p6_universe$n_val_races)` search-set races are reported
"Standard", and classes 2 and 3 together carry
`r p6_fn(sum(p6_rc_pruned$n_races[p6_rc_pruned$label == "class 2-3"]))`
races. Their absence from the results is a fact about the scope of this
series — four All-Weather courses, classes 2 to 5 handicaps, 2006 to 2015 —
not evidence that going or class is uninformative for betting in general.

**Field size is the only race characteristic with real coverage**, and the
band that won, 11 to 12 runners, is
`r p6_fpct(sum(p6_overround_val$n_races[p6_overround_val$field_size %in% 11:12]) / p6_universe$n_val_races, 1)`
of the search set. A rule defined on that band bets about
`r p6_fn(p6_row(p6_round3_ranks$table, "win", "P4 / field size 11-12")$test_bets)`
times on the test split, which is not enough for its ROI to mean much in
either direction.

**The place prices are a construction and the each-way market is not a
market.** Set out in @sec-forward. The place figures are
discounted-Harville probabilities computed from win prices, not traded place
prices; the each-way figures price a bookmaker product that has no exchange
counterpart. Both are internally consistent across the series and neither is
what the forward strategy in @sec-forward would trade.

**The forward strategy is untested.** @sec-forward is a reading of paper 4's
result plus a market-structure argument. Its two load-bearing assumptions —
that usable size exists at early prices, and that the model beats an early
traded price rather than a compiler's forecast — are not tested anywhere in
this series and cannot be tested on this archive.
